authors: Chun, Jon and Schroeder de Witt, Christian and Elkins, Katherine
title: Comparative Global AI Regulation: Policy Perspectives from the EU, China, and the US
what_it_says: Compares AI regulation in the EU, China and the US, with attention to US federal and state approaches including California SB 1047. Argues the regimes reflect different cultural, political and economic outlooks on safety versus innovation and influence one another.
why_relevant: A recent comparative study of the jurisdictions whose provisions the evidence table codes.

authors: Al-Maamari, Amir
title: Between Innovation and Oversight: A Cross-Regional Study of AI Risk Management Frameworks in the EU, U.S., UK, and China
what_it_says: Compares how the EU, US, UK and China classify AI risk, enforce compliance, structure oversight and handle transparency. Finds the EU emphasises transparency and conformity assessment, the US and UK are flexible but risk fragmentation, and China is centralised with limited external oversight.
why_relevant: Directly comparable cross-jurisdiction study that touches conformity assessment, the closest topic to pre-deployment testing.

authors: Du, Jian
title: Toward Responsible and Beneficial AI: Comparing Regulatory and Guidance-Based Approaches
what_it_says: Uses qualitative content analysis of primary documents from 2017 to 2024 to compare AI governance frameworks of the EU, the US, China and IEEE. Identifies three governance models and proposes a hybrid framework.
why_relevant: Precedent for coding governance documents by content analysis and for separating binding rules from guidance.

authors: Roberts, Huw and Ziosi, Marta and Osborne, Cailean and Saouma, Lama
title: A Comparative Framework for AI Regulatory Policy
venue_or_publisher: International Centre of Expertise on Artificial Intelligence in Montreal (CEIMIA)
what_it_says: Proposes a seven category framework for analysing how governments regulate AI and applies it to Canada, China, the EU, the UK and the USA. Finds the EU and Canada favour centralised horizontal hard law while the others use more sector specific, lighter touch measures.
why_relevant: A coding framework for comparing regulatory approaches, relevant to the paper's own coding scheme.

title: National AI policies & strategies
what_it_says: Online database of national AI policy initiatives covering more than 1,000 initiatives from 69 countries, territories and the EU, browsable by country, policy instrument and target group. The page shows an access date of 17/11/2024; the year 2021 is taken from its citation line.
why_relevant: The main existing tracker of national AI policy, against which a provision level evidence table can be positioned.

title: The 2025 AI Index Report
venue_or_publisher: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (Stanford HAI)
what_it_says: Landing page for the annual report; its Chapter 6 teaser says advancing AI capabilities have drawn policymakers' attention and AI related policies are rising worldwide. Specific regulatory findings were not on the page.
why_relevant: Standard annual source for counts and trends in AI policy; a baseline for describing the policy landscape.

authors: Raji, Inioluwa Deborah and Smart, Andrew and White, Rebecca N. and Mitchell, Margaret and Gebru, Timnit and Hutchinson, Ben and Smith-Loud, Jamila and Theron, Daniel and Barnes, Parker
title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
what_it_says: Argues external audits happen after deployment and leave developers without ways to find harms earlier. Proposes an internal auditing framework spanning the development lifecycle whose stage documents combine into an audit report.
why_relevant: Foundational internal audit framework that frames pre-deployment testing as an accountability practice.

authors: Birhane, Abeba and Steed, Ryan and Ojewale, Victor and Vecchione, Briana and Raji, Inioluwa Deborah
title: AI auditing: The Broken Bus on the Road to AI Accountability
venue_or_publisher: IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML) 2024 (to appear, per arXiv listing)
what_it_says: Sorts AI audit work by the actors who do it and finds that only some audits achieve their accountability aims. Identifies the design, methods and institutional context that make audits effective.
why_relevant: Explains why audit requirements on paper may not produce accountability, which bears on reading testing provisions.

authors: Casper, Stephen and Ezell, Carson and Siegmann, Charlotte and Kolt, Noam and others (21 authors listed on page)
title: Black-Box Access is Insufficient for Rigorous AI Audits
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated on page)
what_it_says: Examines limits of audits that only query a system and see outputs, compared with audits given access to internals or development information. Argues that audit results need disclosure of the auditor's access and methods, and discusses safeguards for deeper access.
why_relevant: Access level is a design feature that a testing provision can specify or leave silent; useful for the coding scheme.

authors: Mökander, Jakob and Schuett, Jonas and Kirk, Hannah Rose and Floridi, Luciano
title: Auditing large language models: a three-layered approach
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated on page)
what_it_says: Proposes auditing at three levels: technology providers, pre-release models and LLM based applications. Argues this helps manage ethical and social risks while acknowledging the limits of auditing.
why_relevant: Places pre-release model testing inside a layered audit structure, a useful distinction for classifying provisions.

authors: Ojewale, Victor and Steed, Ryan and Vecchione, Briana and Birhane, Abeba and Raji, Inioluwa Deborah
title: Towards AI Accountability Infrastructure: Gaps and Opportunities in AI Audit Tooling
what_it_says: Maps the AI audit tool ecosystem through a landscape analysis of 390 tools and interviews with 35 practitioners. Finds most tools support evaluation and standards management while tools for harms discovery, audit communication and advocacy are scarce.
why_relevant: Evidence on the practical tooling that checklist or testing requirements assume exists.

authors: Shevlane, Toby and Farquhar, Sebastian and Garfinkel, Ben and Phuong, Mary and Whittlestone, Jess and others (21 authors listed on page)
title: Model evaluation for extreme risks
what_it_says: Argues for evaluating models for dangerous capabilities and for propensity to misuse them. Proposes building such evaluations into governance for training, deployment, transparency and security.
why_relevant: The main reference linking pre-deployment model evaluation to governance decisions.

authors: Liang, Percy and Bommasani, Rishi and Lee, Tony and others (50 authors listed on page)
title: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
what_it_says: Presents HELM, which maps use cases and evaluation criteria and evaluates 30 models across 42 scenarios on seven metrics. Releases prompts, completions and a toolkit and intends the benchmark to be updated continually.
why_relevant: Representative holistic evaluation standard that government testing guidance may reference.

authors: Reuel, Anka and Bucknall, Benjamin and Casper, Stephen and Fist, Timothy and Soder, Lisa and others (33 authors listed on page)
title: Open Problems in Technical AI Governance
what_it_says: Defines technical AI governance as technical analysis and tools that support oversight, gives a taxonomy of open problems and a partial catalogue for researchers and funders.
why_relevant: Situates evaluation and verification methods inside the governance problem the paper addresses.

authors: Anderljung, Markus and Barnhart, Joslyn and Korinek, Anton and Leung, Jade and O'Keefe, Cullen and others (24 authors listed on page)
title: Frontier AI Regulation: Managing Emerging Risks to Public Safety
what_it_says: Argues frontier models are hard to regulate because capabilities emerge unexpectedly and spread. Proposes standard setting, registration and reporting, and compliance mechanisms, with initial safety standards including pre-deployment risk assessment and post-deployment monitoring.
why_relevant: Names pre-deployment risk assessment as a regulatory standard, matching the provisions the evidence table codes.

authors: Feffer, Michael and Sinha, Anusha and Deng, Wesley H. and Lipton, Zachary C. and Heidari, Hoda
title: Red-Teaming for Generative AI: Silver Bullet or Security Theater?
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, 7(1), 421-437
what_it_says: Reviews industry red-teaming and related research and finds practices vary widely in goals, systems tested, settings and decisions informed. Warns that treating red-teaming as a cure-all risks symbolic security work and offers a question bank to guide efforts.
why_relevant: Supports treating mentions of red teaming in policy texts as underspecified unless scope and criteria are stated.

authors: Longpre, Shayne and Kapoor, Sayash and Klyman, Kevin and Ramaswami, Ashwin and Bommasani, Rishi and others (23 authors listed on page)
title: Position: A Safe Harbor for AI Evaluation and Red Teaming
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 235:32691-32710
what_it_says: Says researchers who test generative AI fear account suspension or legal action because company policies can penalise good faith testing. Urges developers to give legal and technical protections for public interest safety research.
why_relevant: Shows that who may test, and under what protection, is itself a governance question for testing provisions.

authors: Bengio, Yoshua and Mindermann, Sören and Privitera, Daniel and Besiroglu, Tamay and Bommasani, Rishi and others (about 100 authors listed on page)
title: International AI Safety Report
what_it_says: Synthesises current research on advanced AI capabilities, risks and ways to make systems safer, produced by about 100 independent experts at the request of countries attending the Bletchley summit.
why_relevant: Intergovernmental evidence base for what safety evaluation can and cannot currently establish.

authors: Perez, Ethan and Huang, Saffron and Song, Francis and Cai, Trevor and Ring, Roman and Aslanides, John and Glaese, Amelia and McAleese, Nat and Irving, Geoffrey
title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
what_it_says: Uses one language model to generate test cases that elicit harmful replies from another, scored by an offensive content classifier. Found tens of thousands of offensive responses from a 280B parameter chatbot and other harms such as leaked training data.
why_relevant: Technical basis for automated red teaming, which some provisions mention without defining.

authors: Weidinger, Laura and Rauh, Maribeth and Marchal, Nahema and Manzini, Arianna and Hendricks, Lisa Anne and others (13 authors listed on page)
title: Sociotechnical Safety Evaluation of Generative AI Systems
what_it_says: Proposes a three layer framework of capability, human interaction and systemic impact evaluation, surveys existing safety evaluations and identifies three gaps in current practice.
why_relevant: Gives a layered vocabulary for what a pre-deployment test is evaluating, usable as a coding dimension.

authors: Phuong, Mary and Aitchison, Matthew and Catt, Elliot and Cogan, Sarah and Kaskasoli, Alexandre and others (27 authors listed on page)
title: Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities
what_it_says: Introduces dangerous capability evaluations on persuasion and deception, cyber security, self-proliferation and self-reasoning and pilots them on Gemini 1.0 models. Finds no strong dangerous capabilities but some early warning signs.
why_relevant: Example of a developer run pre-deployment evaluation of the kind safety frameworks require.

authors: Veale, Michael and Zuiderveen Borgesius, Frederik
title: Demystifying the Draft EU Artificial Intelligence Act
what_it_says: Explains the April 2021 AI Act proposal using research on AI practices and EU product safety regulation. Finds the risk tiers sensible but argues some provisions have unexpected effects and that enforcement and maximum harmonisation raise concerns.
why_relevant: Early critical account of conformity assessment and standards under the AI Act.

authors: Mokander, Jakob and Axente, Maria and Casolari, Federico and Floridi, Luciano
title: Conformity Assessments and Post-market Monitoring: A Guide to the Role of Auditing in the Proposed European AI Regulation
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (journal not named on page)
what_it_says: Explains conformity assessment and post-market monitoring in the proposed AI Act in auditing terms. Argues the Act aims to create a continent wide auditing ecosystem and recommends seven amendments, including checkable criteria and safeguards for self-conducted checks.
why_relevant: Directly addresses conformity assessment and the weakness of self assessment.

authors: Gornet, Mélanie and Maxwell, Winston
title: The European approach to regulating AI through technical standards
what_it_says: Examines how the AI Act borrows harmonised standards and CE marking from product safety and extends them to fundamental rights. Argues standards cannot certify compliance with rights that depend on context and judicial determination, though they can encourage good governance practice.
why_relevant: Core critique of harmonised standards as a route to demonstrating testing compliance.

authors: Wachter, Sandra
title: Limitations and Loopholes in the EU AI Act and AI Liability Directives: What This Means for the European Union, the United States, and Beyond
what_it_says: Argues lobbying weakened the AI Act, which relies heavily on self-regulation, self-certification, weak oversight and broad exemptions. Also argues the liability directives cover mainly material harm and propose ways to close gaps.
why_relevant: Supports the paper's concern with self assessment and exemptions in testing obligations.

authors: Tabassi, Elham
title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
venue_or_publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST AI 100-1)
what_it_says: Landing page describes a voluntary framework to help organisations that design, develop, deploy or use AI identify and manage AI risks across sectors. The page did not itself describe the framework functions or testing, evaluation, verification and validation.
why_relevant: The primary US reference that testing provisions elsewhere are often benchmarked against.

authors: Gilardi, Fabrizio and Alizadeh, Meysam and Kubli, Maël
title: ChatGPT Outperforms Crowd-Workers for Text-Annotation Tasks
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (DOI shown on page: PNAS)
what_it_says: On 2,382 tweets, ChatGPT zero shot accuracy beat crowd workers on four of five annotation tasks and showed higher intercoder agreement than both crowd workers and trained annotators, at about one twentieth the cost.
why_relevant: Evidence used to justify LLM first pass coding of provisions.

authors: Ziems, Caleb and Held, William and Shaikh, Omar and Chen, Jiaao and Zhang, Zhehao and Yang, Diyi
title: Can Large Language Models Transform Computational Social Science?
what_it_says: Evaluates 13 language models on about two dozen computational social science benchmarks zero shot. Finds they fall short of the best fine-tuned classifiers but reach fair agreement with human labelers.
why_relevant: Calibrates expectations for LLM agreement with humans on text classification.

authors: Reiss, Michael V.
title: Testing the Reliability of ChatGPT for Text Annotation and Classification: A Cautionary Remark
what_it_says: Found ChatGPT labels of German website texts varied with temperature, instruction wording and repeated identical inputs, often below accepted reliability thresholds. Majority voting over repeated runs improved consistency; concludes validation against human labels is needed.
why_relevant: Motivates repeated runs and human validation when an LLM codes provisions.

authors: Törnberg, Petter
title: ChatGPT-4 Outperforms Experts and Crowd Workers in Annotating Political Twitter Messages with Zero-Shot Learning
what_it_says: Tests ChatGPT-4 on classifying the party of US politicians' tweets and finds it more accurate and reliable than expert coders and MTurk workers, with equal or lower bias.
why_relevant: Another data point on LLM versus expert coder accuracy in content analysis.

authors: Tan, Zhen and Li, Dawei and Wang, Song and Beigi, Alimohammad and Jiang, Bohan and others (10 authors listed on page)
title: Large Language Models for Data Annotation and Synthesis: A Survey
what_it_says: Surveys LLM based annotation, covering generating annotations, assessing their quality and using them for training, with a taxonomy of data types, learning strategies and open challenges.
why_relevant: Survey to cite for the state of LLM annotation methods and quality assessment.

authors: Savelka, Jaromir and Ashley, Kevin D. and Gray, Morgan A and Westermann, Hannes and Xu, Huihui
title: Can GPT-4 Support Analysis of Textual Data in Tasks Requiring Highly Specialized Domain Expertise?
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (DOI prefix indicates ACM; venue not stated on page)
what_it_says: GPT-4 given annotation guidelines performed comparably to well trained law student annotators on interpreting legal concepts in court opinions. Batch prediction cut cost with small accuracy loss; the model was sensitive to prompt formatting.
why_relevant: Closest evidence for LLM coding of legal text with guidelines.

authors: Guha, Neel and Nyarko, Julian and Ho, Daniel and Ré, Christopher and Chilton, Adam and others (40 authors listed on page)
title: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models
venue_or_publisher: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
what_it_says: Introduces a benchmark of 162 tasks across six categories of legal reasoning, built with legal professionals, and evaluates 20 open source and commercial LLMs.
why_relevant: Benchmark for how well LLMs handle legal text tasks like classifying provisions.

authors: McHugh, Mary L.
title: Interrater reliability: the kappa statistic
what_it_says: Explains Cohen's kappa as a correction to percent agreement for chance, ranging from -1 to +1. Argues Cohen's benchmarks are too lenient for health research and suggests stricter standards.
why_relevant: Accessible source for kappa interpretation thresholds and limitations.

authors: Artstein, Ron and Poesio, Massimo
title: Survey Article: Inter-Coder Agreement for Computational Linguistics
what_it_says: The landing page gave citation metadata only (no abstract was shown); the title identifies it as a survey of inter-coder agreement measures for computational linguistics.
why_relevant: Standard reference for agreement coefficients in annotation work in language technology.

title: Computing Krippendorff's Alpha-Reliability
venue_or_publisher: Departmental Papers (ASC), University of Pennsylvania repository (postprint)
what_it_says: Repository record (author field blank on the page) describing alpha as a reliability coefficient for agreement among coders, observers or instruments, originating in content analysis.
why_relevant: The usual citation for how Krippendorff's alpha is computed.

authors: Bujang, Mohamad Adam and Baharum, Nurakmal
title: Guidelines of the minimum sample size requirements for Kappa agreement test
what_it_says: Gives tables of minimum sample sizes for a kappa test at 80% power and alpha below 0.05. Finds required samples are much larger when marginal rating frequencies differ.
why_relevant: Directly addresses how many items are needed to estimate kappa, relevant to small coded samples.

authors: Hughes, John
title: Toward improved inference for Krippendorff's Alpha agreement coefficient
what_it_says: Proposes a better point estimator and a jackknife variance estimator for Krippendorff's alpha, giving interval estimates with much better coverage than customary bootstrap intervals.
why_relevant: Relevant to interval estimation for alpha when the number of coded provisions is limited.

authors: Wongpakaran, Nahathai and Wongpakaran, Tinakon and Wedding, Danny and Gwet, Kilem L.
title: A comparison of Cohen's Kappa and Gwet's AC1 when calculating inter-rater reliability coefficients: a study conducted with personality disorder samples
what_it_says: Compares kappa and Gwet's AC1 on 67 patients and nine raters in pairs. Finds AC1 more stable and less sensitive to prevalence and marginal imbalance.
why_relevant: Supports reporting an alternative coefficient alongside kappa when categories are skewed.

authors: Pérez, Jorge and Díaz, Jessica and Garcia-Martin, Javier and Tabuenca, Bernardo
title: Systematic Literature Reviews in Software Engineering - Enhancement of the Study Selection Process using Cohen's Kappa Statistic
what_it_says: Proposes iterating reviewer criteria until Cohen's kappa exceeds 0.8, after which reviewers screen separately. Reports about 28% time saving on 152 studies.
why_relevant: Shows kappa used as a calibration threshold in document screening with small numbers of items.

title: AI in the United Arab Emirates
venue_or_publisher: OECD.AI Policy Observatory (publisher inferred, not stated on page)
what_it_says: Country page that lists one national AI policy, the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence of 2031, announced in October 2017, aiming to make the UAE a leader in AI.
why_relevant: Tracker entry for the UAE strategy; a starting point for the UAE gap analysis, not an analytical study.

title: Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT
what_it_says: ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 wrote literature reviews on 42 topics and the 636 citations were checked against scholarly sources. Fabricated citations were 55% for GPT-3.5 and 18% for GPT-4, and both erred on real papers.
why_relevant: Quantifies fabricated references, motivating citation verification for this paper's own bibliography.

authors: Chelli, Mikaël and Descamps, Jules and Lavoué, Vincent and Trojani, Christophe and Azar, Michel and Deckert, Marcel and Raynier, Jean-Luc and Clowez, Gilles and Boileau, Pascal and Ruetsch-Chelli, Caroline
title: Hallucination Rates and Reference Accuracy of ChatGPT and Bard for Systematic Reviews: Comparative Analysis
venue_or_publisher: Journal of Medical Internet Research, 26(1), e53164
what_it_says: Tested GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Bard on reproducing references of 11 systematic reviews. Hallucination rates were 39.6%, 28.6% and 91.4% and precision was 9.4%, 13.4% and 0%.
why_relevant: Links hallucinated references to systematic review searching.

authors: Ji, Ziwei and Lee, Nayeon and Frieske, Rita and Yu, Tiezheng and Su, Dan and others (13 authors listed on page)
title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
what_it_says: Reviews how hallucination in text generation is measured and mitigated across tasks such as summarisation, dialogue and question answering, and in large language models.
why_relevant: General background reference for hallucination definitions.

authors: Agrawal, Ayush and Suzgun, Mirac and Mackey, Lester and Kalai, Adam
title: Do Language Models Know When They're Hallucinating References?
what_it_says: Treats fabricated references as an easy to check case of hallucination. Black-box consistency checks show models vary the invented authors across sessions for fake references but name real authors consistently.
why_relevant: Gives a cheap consistency check that could be used to screen suspect references.

authors: Liu, Nelson F. and Zhang, Tianyi and Liang, Percy
title: Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines
what_it_says: Human audit of four generative search engines found only about half of sentences fully supported by citations and about three quarters of citations supporting their sentences.
why_relevant: Evidence that citations attached to AI generated claims often fail to support them.

authors: Athaluri, Sai Anirudh and Manthena, Sandeep Varma and Kesapragada, V S R Krishna Manoj and Yarlagadda, Vineel and Dave, Tirth and Duddumpudi, Rama Tulasi Siri
title: Exploring the Boundaries of Reality: Investigating the Phenomenon of Artificial Intelligence Hallucination in Scientific Writing Through ChatGPT References
what_it_says: ChatGPT wrote proposals on 50 medical topics; of its 178 references, 69 lacked a working DOI and 28 could not be found by Google or DOI.
why_relevant: Early quantification of fabricated references in AI assisted research writing.

authors: Rao, Delip and Callison-Burch, Chris
title: BibTeX Citation Hallucinations in Scientific Publishing Agents: Evaluation and Mitigation
what_it_says: Builds a 931 paper benchmark and finds search enabled frontier models get about 84% of BibTeX fields right but only about half of entries fully correct. Grounding output in a deterministic retrieval tool improves accuracy.
why_relevant: Supports checking every field of a reference against a bibliographic source, not just existence.

authors: Naser, M.Z.
title: How LLMs Cite and Why It Matters: A Cross-Model Audit of Reference Fabrication in AI-Assisted Academic Writing and Methods to Detect Phantom Citations
what_it_says: Checked 69,557 citations from 10 commercial LLMs against CrossRef, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar and found fabrication rates of about 11% to 57% depending on model, field and prompt. Proposes cross-model agreement filters and a text classifier.
why_relevant: Large scale audit of reference fabrication and screening methods.

authors: Rao, Delip and Wong, Eric and Callison-Burch, Chris
title: Detecting and Correcting Reference Hallucinations in Commercial LLMs and Deep Research Agents
what_it_says: Finds about 3 to 13% of citation URLs from LLMs and deep research agents are likely fabricated, and releases an open source tool that separates fabricated from stale links.
why_relevant: Directly relevant to verifying URLs in AI assisted research claims.

authors: Remolina Leon, Nydia and Seah, Josephine
title: How to address the AI Governance discussion? What can we learn from Singapore's AI strategy?
venue_or_publisher: SMU Centre for AI & Data Governance Research Paper No. 2019/03 (working paper)
what_it_says: Examines Singapore's national AI strategy and Model AI Governance Framework, compares it with other jurisdictions and identifies challenges and gaps in AI governance discourse.
why_relevant: Scholarly account of the Singapore model used as a comparator.

authors: Lee Kok Thong, Josh
title: AI Verify: Singapore's AI Governance Testing Initiative Explained
what_it_says: Describes AI Verify as a voluntary testing framework and toolkit combining technical tests with process checks for self-assessment, run internally so data and models stay in the organisation's environment. Aims at verifiability, not defining ethical standards.
why_relevant: Concrete example of a government backed testing toolkit that is voluntary and self assessed.

authors: Harjani, Manoj
title: Where Is Singapore's AI Regulation Headed?
what_it_says: Notes Singapore has no AI specific law and relies on existing legislation and voluntary guidance, including the Model AI Governance Framework and AI Verify, which tests systems against 11 ethics principles. Questions whether this light approach suffices.
why_relevant: Recent commentary on a voluntary testing approach, useful when classifying such provisions as recommended not required.

authors: Spoor, Pat and Airey, Mark and Bennett, Cathy and Greensill, Julie and Williams, Rhys
title: Use of the capture-recapture technique to evaluate the completeness of systematic literature searches
what_it_says: Compared a Medline search with hand searching of one journal for trials from 1984 to 1994, using capture-recapture. Estimated about 160 publications in total with about 2 missed, recommends the approach for all systematic searches while warning that source dependence biases estimates.
why_relevant: Early demonstration of capture recapture for estimating search completeness.

authors: Airey CM and Spoor P and Bennett C and Williams R
title: Using the capture-recapture technique in systematic literature searches
what_it_says: Applied capture-recapture to a decade of one journal, comparing MEDLINE and hand searching: 115 trials found by both, 35 by MEDLINE alone and 8 by hand alone, with about 2.4 estimated missed by both.
why_relevant: Worked numbers for a two source capture recapture estimate.

authors: Motschall, E. and Rücker, G. and Antes, G. and Schumacher, M.
title: The number needed to read: are capture-recapture techniques feasible in searching literature for systematic reviews?
what_it_says: Tested capture-recapture models on a review searched across six databases. Estimates varied widely, and the authors conclude usefulness is doubtful because of manual duplicate identification and model selection problems.
why_relevant: Critical counterpoint on the reliability of capture recapture for searches.

authors: Stelfox HT and Foster G and Niven D and Kirkpatrick AW and Goldsmith CH
title: Capture-mark-recapture to estimate the number of missed articles for systematic reviews in surgery
what_it_says: Estimated about 3 of 40 included articles were missed in a trauma care quality indicator review, with database searches finding roughly 93% of known relevant articles.
why_relevant: Recent applied example of recall estimation for a review search.

authors: Kastner M and Straus SE and McKibbon KA and Goldsmith CH
title: The capture-mark-recapture technique can be used as a stopping rule when searching in systematic reviews
what_it_says: Tested a capture-mark-recapture model (Horizon Estimate) as a stopping rule for searching osteoporosis decision support literature across four databases. Concluded it indicates how close a search is to capturing the literature but needs more research.
why_relevant: Frames recall estimation as a stopping rule for searches.

authors: Kastner M and Straus S and Goldsmith CH
title: Estimating the Horizon of articles to decide when to stop searching in systematic reviews: an example using a systematic review of RCTs evaluating osteoporosis clinical decision support tools
what_it_says: Adapted capture-mark-recapture to estimate how many relevant articles lie beyond those found; the review captured about 68% of known articles with an estimated 592 missing.
why_relevant: Earlier source for the Horizon Estimate approach.

authors: Niwitpong, Sa-aat and Böhning, Dankmar and van der Heijden, Peter G.M. and Holling, Heinz
title: Capture-recapture estimation based upon the geometric distribution allowing for heterogeneity
what_it_says: Develops Chao's lower bound estimator for mixtures of geometric distributions and a censored likelihood estimator for population size from identification counts under heterogeneity.
why_relevant: Statistical background for lower bound population estimates when items differ in capture probability.

authors: Cormack, Gordon V. and Grossman, Maura R.
title: Engineering Quality and Reliability in Technology-Assisted Review
what_it_says: Shows quality defined by a recall threshold reduces to the probability of meeting it, and how any TAR method can be augmented to guarantee reliability at a known review cost. Tested on 555 TREC 2015 Total Recall topics, and proposes stopping criteria.
why_relevant: Recall estimation and stopping criteria in document review.
